chunks: Publicly confirmed: CCI’s global site provides a First Timers form intended to help the church get to know visitors. Public local link pages have also exposed first-time and second-time visit forms. Local operational context supplied for this knowledge base (verify against current campus policy): CCI’s Follow-Up ministry seeks to help first-timers find family, grow in Christ, and become established. The journey should feel relational and pastoral, not like a call centre. Follow-up combines a warm welcome, a personal call or contact where appropriate, invitations to church/community, prayer, relationship-building, and support toward becoming established in the church. The visitor is welcomed and, where they consent, shares contact information through an approved official form. The follow-up team may reach out through the approved channel and agreed contact preferences.
First-timer follow-up (FT)

The team checks how the person is doing, answers questions, prays with them if requested, and helps them connect with a community. The person may be invited to return, join a Meet and Pray group, attend Membership Classes, or explore an appropriate service unit/interest group at the right time. Follow-up records should be kept only in approved systems by authorised team members.
First-timer follow-up (FT)

Internal process notes to validate with current campus/global leadership before turning into an automated instruction: The local operating model has used a four-week follow-up sequence. The first follow-up call is expected to be a real phone call rather than only a text message. The team has used a target of five calls per worker per week. Calls, visits, and other interactions are expected to be logged in the authorised follow-up system. The team has worked with a weekly deadline for entering or completing follow-up activity; exact deadline and time must be confirmed before use. Follow-up should respect a person’s preferred time and consent. A message such as “I’ll call later” should not be treated as a completed call.
Rooted / follow-up tracking terminology

After a defined follow-up period, a person may be moved to an appropriate re-engagement workflow if they have not been reached or established; exact statuses and triggers are internal and should not be exposed publicly.
Rooted / follow-up tracking terminology

CCI websites describe opportunities to serve and promote ministries. At a local campus, volunteers may help welcome guests, support services, communicate information, care for children or teens, organise events, support media, or assist with practical ministry operations. The exact service-unit structure varies by campus. Local operational context supplied for this knowledge base: Olu-Obasanjo campus operations have involved functions such as New Members Integration (NMI), Information Desk, Book Sales, Vendor Management, Membership Class, Data, Welfare, and Event Management. The precise current naming, ownership, and recruitment process should be confirmed with campus leadership. Do not imply every unit is open to every visitor at every time.
Service units and volunteering

If asked “How can I serve?” answer: “That's lovely, fam. CCI has different ways to serve, and the available teams can vary by campus. Please check the current CCI campus link hub or speak with the Information Desk after service. They can point you to the right team and any onboarding steps.”
Service units and volunteering

This section combines local operational context previously supplied by a campus team member with public CCI concepts. It is not a public-facing policy manual. Have the campus/global Follow-Up lead and pastor validate it before automating actions or giving exact operational instructions. It intentionally excludes member-level records, internal URLs, individual worker performance details, private phone numbers, and named accountability lists.
Local operations knowledge for an internal campus assistant

The local aim is to make the reception warm, orderly, and personal. New people should be received with care and guided to the right next step without making the experience feel noisy, confusing, or transactional. Teams supporting the reception may include follow-up/new-members support, information desk, and other units as directed by the campus plan. Local practices discussed by campus teams have included preparing refreshments before guests arrive where feasible, assigning a small and clear set of speakers/assistants, and stationing an assistant where they can guide guests to the next step. These are operational examples, not permanent rules. The current Sunday service lead owns the final plan.
Campus welcome and First Timer (FT) reception

The local Follow-Up culture values care and accountability. The purpose is not simply to tick boxes: people should be helped to find family, grow in Christ, and become established. Calls and visits must be respectful, genuine, and logged in the authorised system by authorised workers. A completed call should mean a real, completed interaction, not only a text or an unfulfilled promise to call.
Follow-Up process principles

Local campus operations involve leads and assistant leads, service unit coordination, and oversight from pastoral leadership. Do not reveal internal personnel decisions, disciplinary processes, private meeting links, or restricted training materials. If a question requires permission (e.g., sharing a system workflow with another church/campus, granting access to a form, or changing an official policy), refer the user to the authorised pastor or process owner. Never infer that public availability of a link equals permission to redistribute private material.
Leadership, approvals, and accountability

names of people listed as defaulters or at risk; individual call rates, visit history, attendance or retention status; private campus-by-campus headcounts or comparative dashboards; internal strike/disciplinary status; staff or volunteer phone numbers unless the campus has explicitly published them for public contact; internal Google Meet links, non-public forms, internal assignment lists, and private WhatsApp groups.
Keep worker performance and reports private

Follow-Up exists to help newcomers feel cared for, become connected to the church family, grow in Christ and become established. It should not feel like cold sales outreach, surveillance, or a call centre. Personal contact must be respectful, transparent and proportionate.
Purpose

A first call should be an actual call when the process requires a call; a text saying “I will call” is not a completed call. Respect a person’s preferred contact time where known and approved. Record interactions accurately in the authorised system; do not fabricate completed calls, visits or outcomes. The local four-week follow-up sequence and ReEngage-after-Week-4 concept are operating notes that must be confirmed against the current official Rooted SOP before use. Local notes reference a target of five calls per week and a Wednesday noon deadline in one process. These are not to be presented as universal CCI policy without current leadership confirmation. Local notes mention a five-FT, four-consecutive-week post-probation expectation. Treat this as an internal local operating expectation subject to current confirmation, not a public church-wide rule.
Local operating principles supplied for this knowledge base

Introduce yourself and identify the church/team honestly. Ask if it is a good time to speak. Listen more than you talk; do not interrogate. Ask what support or next step the person would find useful. Never share one visitor’s details with another visitor. Do not copy contact details into personal spreadsheets, private phones or unapproved groups. Log only the minimum necessary information in the authorised system. Respect “please don’t call/message me” immediately and follow the approved suppression process. Escalate pastoral concerns to authorised leaders without gossiping or broadcasting details.
Good contact practices

Use standardised, factual outcomes where the authorised CRM supports them: Reached — spoke to person; No answer; Busy — asked for callback; Wrong number; Number unavailable; Requested no further contact; Needs pastoral follow-up; Visit scheduled; Visited; Unable to verify identity. Do not mark “Reached” when only a message was sent. Do not include sensitive personal details in a free-text note unless the approved process requires them.
Contact outcome vocabulary

Login or account access issue: authorised system administrator or Information Desk as applicable; never request a password in chat. Missing profile or duplicate: authorised Rooted/CRM admin; do not create a duplicate blindly. No response from a newcomer: follow approved cadence; do not increase contact pressure outside policy. Sensitive prayer/counselling request: route privately to an authorised pastoral/care contact with consent. Safeguarding concern or immediate danger: urgent escalation to the designated safeguarding lead and appropriate emergency help; protect the affected person’s confidentiality. Complaint about a worker or leader: provide the approved confidential reporting route; do not promise a specific outcome.
Escalation matrix

Internal local notes mention monthly MAP reporting and weekly operational coordination. Specific deadlines and formats should be maintained in a separate restricted SOP with a named owner and review date. Do not embed a report spreadsheet, private leader list or member attendance in the public retrieval corpus.
MAP reporting and deadlines

The campus operating context shared for this reference includes multiple connected functions. The exact current unit names, reporting lines, personnel and scope must be maintained by local leadership.
CCI Olu-Obasanjo campus operations: functional map

NMI’s operating purpose in the local context is to support the transition from a person attending a service to feeling welcomed, known, connected and guided towards an appropriate next step. It should coordinate with Follow-Up and the Information Desk rather than treating reception as a separate transaction. Operational responsibilities may include: Helping the campus prepare the first-timer/new-convert reception plan. Confirming who welcomes guests, who explains the next step, and who handles any registration or account-access question. Keeping the reception orderly, warm and relatively low-noise. Ensuring that only authorised people handle personal details or follow-up assignments. Communicating with the Follow-Up lead when a guest needs connection after the service.
New Members Integration (NMI)

Making sure that promises made to a guest—for example, a call, a visit, or information about a group—are handed to an accountable person and not lost between units. NMI must not pressure a person to disclose personal details, imply that giving contact information is the price of being welcome, or promise a specific contact schedule before confirming the person’s preference and the approved process.
New Members Integration (NMI)

The Information Desk is a practical help point. In the local context, people with sign-in problems, CCI App access problems, questions about where to go, or uncertainty about next steps should be directed to the Information Desk during service. The desk should be ready to handle or route questions such as: Where should a first-time visitor go? How does a returning visitor complete the relevant sign-in or form? Who can explain Membership Classes or MAP? Where can someone ask about service units or current programme registration? Who can help when a church application or member profile does not load correctly? Where should an event attendee go for book sales, a celebration enquiry, or a vendor-related question?
Information Desk

System-access rule: the Information Desk must never ask for passwords, one-time passcodes, bank PINs or recovery codes. It should direct a person to the approved sign-in/recovery process. A worker helping with a member profile should use their own authorised account and must not share logins.
Information Desk

Book Sales is a distinct operational function in the campus context. Its readiness matters particularly during special services and programmes when the campus expects increased demand.  Confirm the approved inventory list before the service or programme. Verify displayed prices from the current approved price list rather than memory. Confirm the payment routes authorised for that sale and test that the route or POS process works. Place books and signage before the expected arrival of the speaker or guests when the programme plan requires early readiness. Appoint an authorised person to handle sales records and end-of-day reconciliation. Record stock issued, sold, returned, damaged or missing according to the current finance/stock procedure. Keep personal money separate from church sales funds. Never tell a customer to pay into an unverified personal account.
Book Sales
Escalate price discrepancies, missing stock, failed transfers and refund questions to the designated supervisor.
Book Sales

Vendor Management coordinates approved vendors when food, merchandise, services or other vendor support is required. The function must operate under the authorised procurement and event plan, not on informal assumptions. A suggested checklist includes vendor approval; scope and delivery timing; access/arrival arrangements; power, space and safety requirements; agreed pricing or commission where relevant; hygiene and waste handling for food; service-day communication; and settlement/reconciliation. Only the authorised procurement or finance owner should confirm contractual commitments and payment status.
Vendor Management

For a programme involving several services, food or refreshments for workers should be planned against the approved roster, service count and realistic delivery window. A previous local operating discussion considered using a roster when workers serve more than two services. Treat that as a planning example, not an automatic current policy. Check the latest service plan and budget before promising refreshments or quantities.
Vendor Management

The Membership Class function helps attendees understand the schedule, joining route, course materials and approved follow-up to completion. Public CCI pages describe Membership Classes as an introduction to CCI’s teaching, values, culture and community. The specific local cohort schedule, room, eligibility, attendance requirement and completion process must be verified for each cohort. The team should keep a clear distinction between: Enquiry: the person is interested and wants information. Registration: the required approved sign-up step has been completed. Attendance: presence at a specific class has been recorded under the approved process. Completion: the official completion criteria have been met and recorded.
Membership Class team

Do not tell a person they have completed Membership Class based on a verbal assurance, a single attendance or an incomplete list. Conversely, do not publicly discuss why a named member has not completed a course. Route corrections privately to the authorised administrator.
Membership Class team

The Data function supports accurate records and useful reporting. Data should help ministry teams make sound decisions; it should not become a reason to over-collect information or shame people. The data team’s essential disciplines are: Use a defined reporting period and clearly stated counting rules. Distinguish total physical attendance from first-timer count, second-timer count, new-convert count, online attendance and unique people. Record which service or gathering a count relates to. Identify late submissions, missing data, duplicates, sync delays and corrections transparently. Avoid editing source data merely to make a dashboard look consistent. Maintain audit trails for material corrections. Limit access to named-member reports to the workers who need it. Keep a source-of-truth field and submission timestamp for each metric.
Data and reporting function
Report uncertainty rather than quietly filling missing values with assumptions.
Data and reporting function

A service plan should record at minimum: Service date and service labels (Service 1, Service 2, Service 3 if applicable). Approved start/end times and the time zone. Venue and any special entrance/parking/access note cleared for public release. Worker roster and rotation between services. First-timer reception staffing. Information Desk and account-support coverage. Book Sales opening/readiness and stock arrangement. Approved vendor/refreshment plan. Children's/teens and safeguarding coverage where applicable. Sound, media, projection and power dependencies. Clean-up, reset, lost-property and end-of-service handoff. Any change communicated to people who may rely on an earlier announcement.
Why service planning must be explicit

Local discussion identified reception congestion and rowdiness as an issue to manage. Practical principles include: Prepare seats and approved refreshments before guests are brought into the reception area where feasible. Keep only the number of speakers and assistants required by the plan. Have assistants know their exact positions and handoff tasks before guests arrive. Make one person responsible for explaining the next step, instead of several people speaking at once. Keep an assistant stationed where they can guide guests toward sign-in, seating, a group or the exit as appropriate. Ensure the NMI/Follow-Up team is ready before the service ends rather than assembling the process while guests are waiting. Give a clear non-pressuring explanation of what information is being collected and why.
First-timer reception: reduce congestion without reducing care
Keep a route for someone who does not want to join the reception or does not want later contact. The goal is not to reduce guests to a queue. It is to provide personal care in an orderly setting.
First-timer reception: reduce congestion without reducing care

Local operational notes describe additional coordination when the Apostle or another major guest is expected. The final arrangement must be approved for each visit, but common dependencies include: Confirm who owns the overall event/service plan. Ensure the FT/new-convert reception plan, materials, seating and responsible workers are ready before guests arrive. Confirm Information Desk readiness and the process for handling access/sign-in questions. Prepare Book Sales inventory, prices, display and approved payment process before the guest arrives where sales are expected. Activate Event Management for a camp meeting or other major event when the approved plan requires it. Coordinate vendors only where the event plan calls for them. Check worker movement, meal/refreshment coverage and service resets if the plan contains multiple services.
When a global leader or special guest visits

Confirm who may make announcements or post public information. Use a single updated run sheet so different teams do not act on conflicting times. Close the event with a clear handoff, reconciliation and incident-report route. These points are planning prompts, not proof that every team or vendor is required at every visit. The current event lead decides.
When a global leader or special guest visits

The locally expressed purpose of Follow-Up is to help a person find family, grow in Christ and become established. The operational method should combine genuine care with reliable accountability. It is not a sales pipeline, a call centre script, or a way to pressure someone into membership. A helpful way to model the journey is: Welcome → Consent and correct details → Assignment → Genuine first contact → Ongoing connection → Visits/community → Membership/discipleship next step → Established connection or respectful closure. This is a conceptual journey. Exact statuses and completion rules must match the current Rooted/CRM system and approved SOP.
The outcome the process is designed to support

Before a record is assigned or a worker calls: Confirm the record belongs to the right campus and reporting date. Check for duplicates using the authorised matching rules; do not merge records solely because names look similar. Use only contact information supplied through an approved channel. Check any contact preference, consent or do-not-contact instruction captured in the system. Ensure the assigned worker is permitted to view the record and has the correct campus/team assignment. Check any required safeguarding or pastoral flag through the restricted approved workflow, not by sharing sensitive information in a group chat. Do not assign a person based on assumptions about their age, gender, profession or personal circumstances unless a current approved process explicitly requires a relevant criterion.
Before the first contact

The locally shared expectation is that when the SOP calls for a first call, the worker should actually call rather than log an intention to call or send a message saying “I will call.” A text-only contact must be recorded as a message, not as a completed call. A good first call should: Introduce the worker by name and explain that they are contacting the person on behalf of CCI Olu-Obasanjo/Follow-Up. Confirm they are speaking to the intended person without disclosing church or personal details to an unintended recipient. Ask whether it is a convenient time to speak. Thank the person for visiting and ask about their experience in a warm, non-scripted way. Listen for what the person needs; do not assume they want to become a member immediately. Explain one suitable next step, such as the next service, MAP, Membership Classes or another approved connection route.
First contact

Ask or confirm their preferred contact time/channel where the system and approved consent process allow it. Close politely and avoid making promises the worker cannot keep. If there is no answer, record the actual outcome and follow the approved retry cadence. Do not label a no-answer attempt as a completed conversation. If the number is wrong, stop repeated attempts to that number and raise a data correction.
First contact

The process should respect preferred contact times where known and verified. A preference is not a licence to disclose the person’s details to the entire team. It should be stored only in the authorised system and made visible only to the workers who need it. When a person asks not to be contacted, the worker should acknowledge the request, stop further contact through that channel, and apply the approved suppression/closure process. Workers should not argue, use guilt, recruit other people to continue calling, or mark the person negatively for declining follow-up. If someone prefers a different contact method, follow the current consent and SOP rules. Do not assume that a person’s presence at one service grants unlimited permission for repeated personal messaging.
Respecting contact preferences and boundaries

The locally shared operating context has described a four-week sequence, with a re-engagement stage after Week 4. This must be checked against the current Rooted SOP before being treated as active policy. A conceptual four-week framework can help teams remember the purpose of each stage without inventing a script: Week 1 — Welcome and listen: establish a respectful first connection, thank the visitor, understand their immediate questions and offer a clear next step. Week 2 — Connect: follow up on the first conversation and, where useful, introduce MAP or another suitable community option. Week 3 — Encourage growth: help the person find official teaching, Sunday services, prayer or Membership Classes if they express interest. Week 4 — Review and hand off: check whether they want to stay connected, whether any promised support remains outstanding, and what next step they prefer.
Four-week follow-up sequence and re-engagement

After Week 4 — Re-engagement or closure: use only the approved cadence and contact rules. Re-engagement should not become endless attempts after a clear no-contact request. This is an illustrative framework for knowledge organisation, not a claim that every current Rooted workflow uses these exact weekly goals. The official SOP and current system fields supersede this outline.
Four-week follow-up sequence and re-engagement

Local notes have referenced a requirement for four visits before an FT is considered complete. This is a particularly important rule to verify before embedding as an automation, because status completion may also depend on time, consent, attendance, profile completeness or a newer system configuration. Unless the current SOP says otherwise: Do not mark someone complete merely because a worker says a visit happened. Record actual visit dates/outcomes in the authorised system. Distinguish a scheduled visit from a completed visit. Do not fabricate in-person contact, count a message as a visit, or backdate an interaction to meet a target. Escalate duplicate or impossible histories for administrative review. Do not disclose a person’s visit history outside an authorised workflow.
Visits and “FT complete” status

Log interactions promptly and objectively in the authorised CRM/Rooted system. A minimum useful record, where supported by the approved system, includes date/time, channel, outcome, assigned worker, next action and any approved non-sensitive note. Do not place sensitive pastoral details in general activity notes. Do not maintain shadow contact lists in personal devices or spreadsheets. An accurate record distinguishes: attempted call; connected call; message sent; reply received; visit planned; visit completed; person requested no further contact; incorrect number; referral made; and administrative issue. Do not collapse all of these into “contacted.”
Interaction logging

Person wants prayer: ask whether they would like the approved prayer-request path or a private handoff to an authorised pastoral worker. Person shares abuse, imminent danger or suicidal intent: prioritise immediate safety, use the current safeguarding escalation route and encourage appropriate emergency help. Do not leave a dangerous situation to a normal weekly call queue. Person asks for financial or welfare help: route privately to the authorised welfare team; do not promise assistance. Person complains about a worker: provide the current confidential escalation process; do not investigate in a group chat or promise a finding. Person is angry about repeated contact: apologise for the experience, stop or reduce contact according to their expressed preference, and escalate any data/process issue.
Escalation scenarios

Person says they are already part of another CCI campus: verify campus assignment and use approved transfer/routing procedures rather than creating duplicate profiles. The same person appears multiple times: ask the authorised admin to review matching fields and merge only under the system’s rules.
Escalation scenarios

Local use has included cases where tagged profiles or expected backend information did not appear as anticipated. These symptoms could arise from sync delay, incomplete data, wrong filters, mapping/tagging errors, permissions, a failed form submission or a source-system issue. Do not declare the Rooted backend at fault without evidence. Troubleshooting sequence: Confirm the user is signed into the correct account and campus/branch context. Check the date range, current filter, search spelling and selected record type. Confirm whether the source form or source system contains the record. Check whether the record is already present under a variant name or permitted matching fields; avoid creating a duplicate before searching. Confirm tagging/assignment fields and whether the action was saved successfully.
Missing records, tagging errors and data synchronisation

Record the time, non-sensitive record identifier and exact symptom for the authorised administrator. Ask the system owner to verify sync logs or backend processing through official admin tools. Only re-submit/re-tag when the authorised procedure says it is safe. Do not share full member details or screenshots in public channels while troubleshooting. If a screenshot is necessary, redact contact details and unrelated profiles before sending it to the approved support route.
Missing records, tagging errors and data synchronisation

Member/visitor: own information and public links only. Follow-Up worker: only assigned records and approved interaction functions. Campus/branch administrator: approved branch-level record correction and workflow support. Campus Follow-Up lead: approved team-level supervision and aggregated reporting. Regional/global lead: only the broader views and operations explicitly granted to that role. System administrator: configuration and technical functions, with audit logging. Keep administrative powers separated where feasible. A person who can contact newcomers does not automatically need to download all member data or change completion rules.
Permissions and role model

Local context included CRM onboarding run with the Axios team for leads and assistant leads, with attendance treated as compulsory for that particular session. The session link itself is not a permanent public resource and should not be hard-coded into this document. For future onboarding, record the current date, audience, authorised trainer, approved meeting link, objectives, support route and version of the material. Once the training date has passed, mark the invitation as historical. Do not reuse an old meeting link as if it were the next training.
Training and cross-campus knowledge sharing

Local context also indicates that sharing system training or operational knowledge with another church may require approval from the appropriate pastor/process owner. Before training another campus or external church, confirm whether the content is approved for redistribution, whether a system owner must attend, and which links or datasets must be withheld. Never infer permission merely because someone knows a workflow.
Training and cross-campus knowledge sharing

A recurring local issue has been a difference between physical headcount and the count of records in Rooted. These values need not match because they may represent different populations. Physical headcount may include members, visitors and children; Rooted may contain only people entered into a particular workflow; form completion may be partial; one person may attend multiple services; and data may be entered or synchronised later. The report should clearly define each denominator and avoid implying that Rooted count is the same thing as total Sunday attendance.  Physical attendance/headcount: the number counted onsite under the campus’s approved counting method for the stated service(s) and date. State whether it is a per-service count or a deduplicated total. First-time visitors: people classified as first-time under the current approved definition and captured for the stated date.
Do not combine unlike metrics

Second-time visitors: people classified under the current CCI workflow definition; do not infer from attendance alone unless the data supports it. Rooted records created: number of records created during the period, not necessarily number of people physically present. Contact attempts: actual logged attempts within the period, distinct from successful conversations. Reached/connected people: distinct individuals successfully contacted according to the approved definition. Visits: completed visits, not plans or invitations. Retention: use the official cohort/time-window definition; do not invent one from a raw headcount. Membership Class registration/completion: use the official status definition and cohort window. MAP attendance/reporting: distinguish group reporting submissions from headcount or individual attendance, where the system supports that distinction.
Do not combine unlike metrics

When physical counts and CRM records appear far apart, investigate methodically: Confirm both numbers refer to the same campus, service date and time window. Confirm whether the physical number combines multiple services and whether the Rooted number does. Confirm whether children, workers, online attendance, new converts, second timers and visitors are included in each source. Confirm whether figures count attendances or unique people. Check for missing/late forms, duplicate records, wrong campus tags and incomplete data entry. Confirm that the Rooted report filter and sync date are correct. Check whether any workflow was introduced partway through the reporting period. Document the difference and suspected causes without accusing an individual or campus. Assign an owner and due date for reconciliation. Escalate only after the definitions and extraction steps are reproducible.
Reconciliation before escalation
A dashboard should ideally show separate cards for physical attendance, first-timer count, records created, follow-up contacts, and retention—not display one number as a substitute for another.
Reconciliation before escalation

The local workflow has included Sunday data consolidation by a set evening deadline, transfer to an office/admin review on Monday, and a subsequent leadership submission. Another locally noted deadline has been for regional leads to submit early Monday morning in West Africa Time. These are historical local operating notes and must be reconfirmed before current use. For a reliable report handoff, every report should include: Report title and date range. Campus/region and reporting owner. Submission timestamp in Africa/Lagos time. Data source and extraction timestamp. Definitions of the headline numbers. Missing submissions and whether they are still pending. Corrections since the prior report. Known limitations or sync concerns. The person responsible for follow-up on each unresolved issue.
Weekly data submission and handoff

Local notes have mentioned different deadlines for contact activity, campus reporting and regional reporting. Do not collapse them into one global “Follow-Up deadline.” Maintain a deadline registry with one row per deliverable: Call/contact activity log — Assigned Follow-Up worker — Confirm current SOP; earlier notes referenced a Wednesday noon deadline for a particular task — Africa/Lagos — Follow-Up lead — Needs validation Calls/visits report — Worker/team as defined by current SOP — Earlier notes referenced Friday 9:00 AM for a specific reporting stream — Africa/Lagos — Lead/assistant lead — Needs validation Sunday campus data report — Designated campus data owner — Earlier workflow referenced Sunday 9:00 PM — Africa/Lagos — Campus reporting owner — Needs validation
Deadlines: separate the workflow, not just the date

Regional consolidation — Regional lead/assigned data owner — Earlier workflow referenced Monday 9:00 AM — Africa/Lagos — Regional/global reporting owner — Needs validation MAP monthly report — MAP reporting owner — Use current MAP calendar — Africa/Lagos — Campus/regional MAP owner — Needs validation
Deadlines: separate the workflow, not just the date

Local reporting discussions have referenced call-rate targets, four-week retention, hangout/connection activities and a quarterly campus KPI dashboard. Those labels need an approved metric dictionary with numerator, denominator, population, observation window and data source. A target such as a 95% call rate is not meaningful unless it is clear which assigned people, weeks and contact attempts count. manufacture a score where data is missing; treat unanswered calls as connected conversations; treat messages as calls where the KPI specifies calls; compare campuses with different collection periods or definitions; publicly name campuses or workers as “at risk” from internal dashboards; recommend discipline based solely on a single dashboard statistic; change a target because a system’s default value happens to be different.
KPI interpretation and reporting integrity

When a report is corrected, keep the previous value, the corrected value, the reason, correction timestamp, source of evidence and person/role approving the change. Do not overwrite a report silently. Mark whether the change affects a previously submitted leadership report and whether a corrected version has been redistributed.
Reports and audit trails

The campus MAP directory must be treated as an operational database, not a static announcement. For each group maintain: Campus and approved group name. General geographic area served (not a public home address). Current status: active, paused, merging, newly created or retired. Designated leader/point of contact in a restricted field. Person/role approving the update. Notes about duplicate names or geographic overlap. When areas change, retire or replace an outdated entry rather than simply adding a new row and leaving two conflicting choices. Before deleting anything, follow the approved retention/audit process and check whether existing members need a transition message.
MAP directory maintenance

The local operating context includes recurring MAP reports and the need to monitor participation and submitted information. Use the current approved calendar and form. Distinguish between (a) a report submitted, (b) a MAP meeting held, (c) estimated/recorded attendance, and (d) unique members connected, if all are separately collected. A missing report does not automatically prove no meeting occurred.
MAP reporting

The local structure includes leads and assistant leads. In a healthy process, the lead is responsible for direction and delivery, while the assistant lead supports execution, continuity, communication and follow-through. Exact role descriptions may vary by team. Make the division of responsibility clear for each recurring deliverable so that an absence, change of assignment or leadership transition does not interrupt care for visitors. A worker-facing assistant may explain the approved responsibilities, remind a person of a current task, or provide a checklist. It should not appoint leaders, reassign a person, approve an exception, or decide someone has failed a role unless such an action is explicitly part of a permissioned official workflow.
Lead and assistant-lead responsibilities

Local accountability notes have included attendance expectations for leads and assistant leads and a method for verifying whether a required meeting was attended. If attendance is used for accountability, the process should be transparent, consistently applied and appealable. The verifier should work from the approved attendance record, not rumours or memory.
Meetings and attendance

Local notes have described a strike-based accountability approach and a possible reassignment after repeated strikes, with later guidance indicating that a probation stage may not apply in every case. These are leadership-sensitive rules and may have changed. They must not be treated as automatic universal policy without a current approved document.
Strikes, probation and reassignment

Use the current deadline register rather than a remembered deadline. If a deadline has been missed, distinguish an incomplete activity from a missing log entry or technical failure. Ask the worker to correct records honestly; do not encourage backdating or marking work complete when it was not completed.
Due dates for calls and visits

Accountability should coexist with care. A team member may be unable to meet a target because of an illness, travel, family emergency, changed schedule, system access issue or an unclear assignment. The approved process should make room for a private conversation, support or reassignment when appropriate without erasing required standards. Do not expose private reasons for absence to the whole team.
Team care and workload

Local context has included campus-level review and auditing of service/Follow-Up processes, data completeness and operational alignment. An audit should identify process gaps, improve consistency, and support people—not become a public ranking exercise. A typical approved audit framework may cover: Whether current SOPs exist and have a named owner. Whether physical attendance and digital data definitions are documented. Whether first-timer and second-timer workflows are understood. Whether all required interactions are recorded in the system. Whether MAP directories and report routes are current. Whether worker onboarding and access reviews are completed. Whether private data is stored only in approved systems. Whether unit responsibilities, handoffs and backup owners are clear. Whether pending corrections have an owner and due date.
Purpose of an audit
Whether changes since the prior review were implemented and tested.
Purpose of an audit

A regional/global lead may conduct a physical visit where practical, but any audit must be authorised and appropriately scoped. Checklists should state the sample, dates and evidence reviewed. A missing record should be logged as a finding for verification, not treated as proof that an action did not happen. Where system data is unavailable due to permissions or sync, record the limitation instead of asking workers to send uncontrolled exports.
Audit sampling and physical checks

An operational announcement should answer: who is expected to act; what is happening; date; time and time zone; location/link; whether attendance/action is compulsory or optional; what to prepare; the deadline; the owner/contact role; and what to do if someone has a genuine conflict or cannot access the system. For reminders, preserve the essential facts and do not create urgency through threats or guilt. For a change, state what has changed and which previous instruction is superseded. Do not repost a past event invite without verifying its date and link.
Recommended announcement fields

The campus style should feel like family: warm, human and welcoming, while still clear about responsibilities. Avoid overly robotic language or treating people as a contact database. Acknowledge the person, give the practical next step and state any uncertainty plainly. Humour may be appropriate in internal team banter, but not when a person is grieving, distressed, asking for welfare help or reporting harm.
Tone standard

Visitor cannot sign in — Confirm correct official link and basic connection; direct on-site issues to the Information Desk — Information Desk or official application support — Ask for password/OTP or handle another person’s login Worker cannot access Rooted/CRM — Check approved account, role, campus context and current service notice — Authorised system administrator — Bypass permissions or share credentials Profile/tag missing — Search with approved filters; check source form and sync timing — Rooted/CRM administrator — Create duplicate profile as the first step Form/dashboard not updating — Record timestamp and non-sensitive error description; check official status/process — System owner — Claim a root cause without evidence

Service time/location conflict — Compare latest approved campus announcement and official live link hub — Campus communications/admin — Choose a historical schedule and state it as current Giving or book-sale payment issue — Stop and verify using an official source — Finance/authorised Book Sales owner — Invent account details or direct to a private account MAP link not working — Open current official campus Linktree/MAP directory — MAP coordinator — Reveal private meeting address or member roster Personal data sent to wrong place — Stop further sharing; notify authorised data/privacy owner — Campus administrator/process owner — Repost, forward or copy data into another group
Local technical support and operational issue routing

A useful incident note includes the category, time, system/page, error message, steps already attempted and non-sensitive reference ID. Avoid attaching broad screenshots or full exports. Technical logs and identifiers should be shared only with the approved administrator.
